Then when it rains, water can quickly fill these cracks and cause problems. Freeze-thaw cycles in colder regions can also make ground unstable by repeatedly expanding and contracting the soil.

Signs of Unstable Ground

When we're working with heavy machinery, spotting the signs of unstable ground early can save us from a real pickle. Let's look at what we need to keep an eye out for.

Tension Cracks

One of the first signs of trouble is tension cracks appearing in the ground. These are like nature's warning system - they usually show up before a major collapse. You might spot these cracks about 0.5 to 0.75 times the depth of your excavation away from the edge. For example, if you're digging a 2-metre deep hole, look for cracks about 1-1.5 metres back from the edge.

Ground Movement and Bulging

If you notice any soil moving or bulging, especially at the bottom of an excavation, that's a massive red flag. It's like watching a balloon slowly inflate - if the sides of your excavation start bulging outward, it means the ground is under too much pressure and might fail. The soil at the bottom might also start pushing upward, which we call "heave."

Water Warnings

Water can tell us a lot about ground stability. Keep an eye out for:

  • Water seeping from the sides of excavations
  • Sudden changes in water levels
  • Boiling or bubbling in the soil at the bottom of excavations
  • New wet patches appearing where they weren't before

These water signs are like a tap that won't turn off properly - they might start small, but they can quickly become a major problem.

Changes in Nearby Structures

Sometimes the ground gives us indirect signs of instability. Look for new cracks in nearby buildings or structures, leaning trees or poles, or doors and windows that suddenly don't close properly. These changes are like dominos - when one thing starts moving, it affects everything connected to it.

Sound and Feel

Experienced operators often talk about how unstable ground "feels" different. You might notice your machine behaving differently - maybe it feels less stable or makes different sounds when moving. Trust your gut on this one - if something feels off, it probably is.

What To Do When You Spot These Signs Right, so you've spotted some warning signs - what now? Here's what any good operator should do:

Stop Work Immediately

If you notice any of these warning signs, stop work straight away. It's better to pause for a few minutes to assess the situation than to risk a collapse. Think of it like pulling over when you hear a weird noise in your car - better safe than sorry!

Assess and Report

Take a good look at what's happening and report it to your supervisor. Document what you've noticed - photos can be really helpful here. This information might be crucial for figuring out what's causing the problem and how to fix it.

Implement Safety Measures

Sometimes you'll need to take immediate action to prevent accidents:

  • Move machinery and materials away from the affected area
  • Put up barriers to keep people away from dangerous zones
  • Cover excavations if there's a risk of rain making things worse

Get Expert Help

Some ground stability problems need an expert's eye. A geotechnical engineer can assess the situation and recommend the best way to proceed safely. They're like doctors for the ground - they can diagnose the problem and prescribe the right treatment.

Prevention is Better Than Cure

The best way to deal with unstable ground is to prevent problems before they start. Always check ground conditions before starting work, follow proper excavation procedures, and never take shortcuts with safety. Remember, we're not just protecting ourselves, but also our workmates and any nearby people or property.

Remember mate, when it comes to ground stability, it's always better to be a bit too cautious than not cautious enough. One small oversight could lead to a major collapse, and nobody wants that on their watch. Keep these signs in mind, trust your instincts, and always prioritize safety over speed.

And that's the lot! By understanding what makes ground unstable and knowing what signs to watch for, we can all work more safely and effectively. Keep your eyes peeled, stay safe, and don't hesitate to speak up if something doesn't look right!

Title: Review: Genie GS-1432m and GS-1932m slab scissor lifts
Content:
A pair of compact electric scissors aimed at indoor access work, where weight, width, and noise matter as much as reach.

The GS-1432m and GS-1932m sit at the small end of Genie's slab scissor range, and they are built for a specific job: low-level indoor access on smooth, level floors where the lift has to fit through a standard doorway, sit lightly on sensitive flooring, and not deafen anyone working nearby. The "m" in the model number signals the metric build for non-US markets, so NZ buyers and hirers are looking at the right machines. The 1432m gives you 4.30m of platform height indoors (6.30m working height); the 1932m gives you 5.55m indoor platform height (7.55m working height). Outdoors those drop to 3.66m and 4.57m platform heights respectively, because the rated wind envelope is smaller.

Size and weight

This is where these machines earn their place over larger scissors. Stowed length is 1.40m, width is 0.81m (32 inches), and stowed machine height is 1.88m for the 1432m and 1.97m for the 1932m. That means they fit through a standard 820mm doorway with the fixed rails in place — no folding rails, no service lift required. For retail fit-outs, supermarket maintenance, museum installation, and similar work in occupied buildings, this matters.

Weight is the other big number. The 1432m comes in at 900kg, the 1932m at 1,179kg. Tyre contact pressure is 988 kPa on the 1432m and 1,133 kPa on the 1932m, with occupied floor pressure at 9.73 kPa and 12.14 kPa respectively. If you are operating on raised flooring, in a heritage building, or on a polished concrete slab you want preserved, those numbers still need to be checked against the floor loading data for the space. Don't assume "scissor lift" means "safe for any floor".

Reach and capacity

Platform capacity is 227kg unextended and 113kg when the 0.60m slide-out deck is extended. Indoor occupancy is two; outdoor is one. The slide-out is genuinely useful — it takes the outside platform length from 1.40m to 2.00m — but bear in mind that with the deck extended your tool and material weight allowance drops sharply. Two operators plus a couple of moderate tool kits and you're close to the indoor limit before you've put any materials on the deck.

Both machines are drivable at full height. On the 1932m at 5.55m platform height that is genuinely useful and not always offered at this size, particularly when you are walking the lift along a wall or a run of high racking rather than lowering and re-positioning between every move. Drive speed is 4 km/h stowed and 0.8 km/h raised. Gradeability is 25% (14°) but that applies stowed only.

Power and drivetrain

The E-Drive system uses dual sealed AC drive motors on the front wheels rather than hydraulic wheel motors. The practical effects are fewer hydraulic hoses to leak, longer runtime per charge, and lower running noise. Sound pressure at both the ground and platform workstations is rated under 70 dBA — quiet enough that the lift itself is not the limiting factor for working in occupied retail, schools, or offices.

Standard power is 24V DC from two 12V 115Ah flooded lead acid (FLA) batteries. AGM 115Ah is standard on the S+ build, with 132Ah and 150Ah options. For a hire fleet or a busy in-house operation, AGM is worth the upgrade — no electrolyte topping up, less ventilation fuss, and generally a longer service life under heavy duty cycles. Drive cut-out while charging is standard on the S spec; on S+ and Build to Order it becomes an option, which is worth confirming at order.

Safety features

Standard fit on both machines includes a tilt sensor (cut-out at 3° front-to-back, 1.5° side-to-side), platform load sense, pothole protection that drops to a 0.75-inch (1.9cm) ground clearance when deployed, descent/tilt/motion alarm, dual LED flashing beacons, dual front wheel electric brakes, and an auxiliary platform lowering control at ground level. The platform control guard (PCON) and the SmartLink dual-zone control system are also standard, as is the Lift Tools integrated access deck (the step at the rear for getting in and out).

The tilt sensor cut-out is tighter side-to-side than front-to-back, which reflects the stability geometry of a narrow scissor; pay attention to it on uneven slab. The platform load sense system will prevent elevation with an overloaded platform, but it does not replace knowing the rated capacity before you start loading materials at height.

Standards and NZ context

The 2026 spec sheet cites ANSI A92.20 and CSA B354.6, which are the American and Canadian MEWP design standards. For NZ, you'll want to confirm the imported machine carries the CE marking and conforms to AS/NZS 1418.10 for design, and that your safe-use systems are aligned with AS/NZS 2550.10. Operator competency is a separate question: NZQA unit standards in the 23960–23966 range cover MEWP operation, and the EWPA "Yellow Card" or an IPAF PAL Card are the practical training tickets your hire desk or H&S officer will be asking for. Buying or hiring a slab scissor without confirming the operator side of this is a common gap.

Where the trade-offs are

The compact footprint is the whole point of these machines, and it does limit what you can do with them. Outdoor work is single-occupant only, the rated outdoor platform heights are noticeably lower than indoor, and the solid non-marking tyres are excellent on warehouse concrete and showroom flooring but unforgiving on anything rough. If you need to move between an indoor job and an unsealed yard regularly, a rough-terrain scissor or a different machine class is the right answer.

Lift Connect telematics and the Lift Guard zone lighting and white noise alarm features are Build to Order rather than standard. If you are buying for a hire fleet where telematics is part of how you manage utilisation and service intervals, factor that into the spec discussion at order time rather than discovering it later.

For the indoor 4–6m platform-height bracket where a larger scissor either won't fit through the door or puts too much load on the floor, these are well-suited machines. The E-Drive system and the noise rating make them genuinely usable in occupied buildings, and the standard safety fit-out is appropriate for the class.

Title: Review: JLG H340AJ hybrid articulating boom lift
Content:
A 10.33-metre articulating boom that runs on batteries indoors, recharges itself with a diesel generator outdoors, and drives across rough ground on four independent electric motors. On paper, the H340AJ is JLG's answer to a problem most fleets know well — the awkward middle ground where a job needs the cleanliness of an electric scissor and the terrainability of a diesel boom on the same day.

What it is

The H340AJ is the hybrid version of JLG's 340AJ articulating boom. The working envelope is modest by boom-lift standards: 10.33 m platform height, 6.06 m horizontal outreach, 5.17 m up-and-over clearance, and a 227 kg platform capacity. The articulating boom carries a 1.22 m jib with 139 degrees of articulation (+79, -60), and the platform rotates 180 degrees hydraulically. Swing is 355 degrees non-continuous.

The drivetrain is where it earns the "hybrid" label. Four independent electric-drive motors power the wheels, fed by eight 12 V / 100 Ah AGM batteries. A Kubota Z482 11.1 kW Tier 4 Final diesel generator sits on board to recharge the batteries when they get low. The machine never drives directly off the diesel — the engine is purely a generator. That distinction matters, because it's why the unit can run on battery alone inside a building and then top itself up outside without an external charger.

Drive speed lowered is 5.95 km/h, gradeability is 45%, and ground bearing pressure tops out at 4.5 kg/cm². It weighs 4,472 kg in base configuration, and machine width is 1.93 m with a 1.87 m wheelbase and 26 cm of ground clearance. Tailswing is 5.08 cm, which is effectively zero — useful when working close to walls or in tight bays.

What's good about it

The four-wheel electric drive is the headline. Most hybrid booms in this size class are biased toward smooth-floor work and struggle the moment you put them on a building site with cut-up ground. Independent electric motors at each wheel, combined with oscillating axle and 45% gradeability, mean the H340AJ can go where its diesel-only sibling goes. That's the real test — and on the spec sheet, JLG is claiming parity.

The dual-mode operation is genuinely useful, not a gimmick. Run on batteries indoors where you can't have diesel exhaust (food production, warehousing, retail fitouts, hospitals, anywhere with poor ventilation). Drive outside, let the generator run, and the batteries top up while you work. No charging downtime, no swapping units mid-day, no hauling a second machine to site.

Standard kit is well-thought-out. The Control ADE® system, ClearSky Smart Fleet hardware (CS550 telematics beacon), platform console machine status light panel, all-motion alarm, SkyGuard SkyLine™ secondary guarding, 4-degree tilt cut-out, oscillating axle, and rapid-replaceable platform with self-closing gate all come standard. The 110 V AC and 12 V DC outlets in the platform are there, along with USB-A and USB-C charging — small thing, but operators notice when they're not present.

The ClearSky Smart Fleet integration is worth a mention because it's now standard on most JLG equipment. Two-way telematics, wireless diagnostics from the mobile app, real-time machine health data on the web portal, and an API if you want to feed the data into your existing fleet management system. For a hire company or a fleet manager running mixed JLG kit, this is the kind of feature that justifies itself over a couple of breakdown call-outs.

What to watch out for

The H340AJ is not a tall machine. 10.33 m platform height puts the working height around 12.3 m, which is fine for two-storey indoor work, light commercial fitouts, ceiling-grid work, signage, and most facade jobs up to about three storeys. For anything taller, you're looking at the larger units in the range. Don't spec this one and then find out on site that it won't reach.

The 227 kg platform capacity is single-person-plus-tools or a tight two-person rating. If your crew works in pairs with material at height — glaziers carrying a panel, signage installers with brackets and a sign — check the weight before committing. Two operators plus PPE is roughly 200 kg before tools.

The diesel generator still produces emissions and noise, just less of both. If the job spec says "zero emissions" (some hospital and food-processing environments), this isn't the right machine — you want a fully electric unit. The hybrid is for jobs that are mostly indoors but spill outside, or mostly outdoors with indoor segments. It's not a replacement for a pure electric boom on a true emissions-controlled site.

Foam-filled tyres are standard (9 x 20). If the job is on a polished concrete floor or epoxy, you'll want to spec the non-marking option. Easy to miss at order time and expensive to fix afterwards.

Hypothetical situations where it earns its keep

Supermarket refurbishment, trading hours. The store stays open while one aisle is closed off for ceiling-grid replacement. Diesel booms are out — you can't run an internal combustion engine in a supermarket with customers in it. A pure electric scissor doesn't have the up-and-over reach to clear shelving. The H340AJ runs on batteries indoors, articulates over the shelving, and gets recharged in the carpark between shifts.

Light industrial fitout, mixed indoor-outdoor work. A new warehouse is being commissioned. Internal work involves running cable trays at 9 m, hanging light fittings, and final commissioning of HVAC. External work involves signage, downpipes, and gutter checks. One machine handles both jobs across a two-week programme, with the generator topping up the batteries during the outdoor phases.

Hospital or aged-care facility maintenance. Reaching ceiling-mounted plant in a corridor where patients and residents are moving through. Battery operation keeps the noise and exhaust out of the occupied space. The 1.93 m machine width and 5.08 cm tailswing matter here — you can position close to walls without swinging the counterweight into a doorway.

Stadium or arena event prep. Rigging lights and signage on a curved facade or inside a concourse. Up-and-over reach of 5.17 m gets the platform over barriers and seating. Indoor concourses get battery operation; outdoor work runs the generator. No second machine required.

Telecommunications cabinet and small-cell installation. Roadside cabinets and pole-mounted equipment up to 10 m. The hybrid runs quietly enough to work in residential streets without complaints, and the four-wheel drive gets it onto the grass verge without bogging down.

Film and television set work. Lighting rigs, camera platforms, and overhead grip on indoor sets. Battery operation means no generator hum picked up by the sound recordist, no exhaust in the set, and no expensive cable runs from a remote generator. Drive it from the truck on batteries, work the set, drive it back, run the generator while it's parked.

Where it sits in the picture

If your work is consistently outdoors and you don't need clean operation indoors, a diesel boom is cheaper and simpler. If your work is consistently indoors on clean floors and you don't need real terrainability, a slab electric is cheaper still. The H340AJ exists for the jobs that don't sit cleanly in either category — and there are more of those jobs every year as zero-emission zones, after-hours work in occupied buildings, and noise restrictions push fleets to think about which machine actually goes on each booking.

For operators, training on the H340AJ is the same as any other articulating MEWP. The relevant NZQA unit standards for MEWP operation are 23960–23966, and AS2550.10 is the relevant standard for design and use. WorkSafe expects operators to be trained and assessed before being put on the machine, and the dual-mode operation doesn't change that — but it does add one thing worth covering in the site induction: when the generator will and won't start automatically, and what to do if it kicks in while you're working in an enclosed space.

The H340AJ isn't trying to be the biggest or the tallest. It's trying to be the machine that doesn't need a second machine on the same job. On the spec sheet, it makes a strong case for that.

Title: Skyjack SJ82 T and SJ86 T: a telescopic boom review for NZ operators
Content:
These are big telescopic booms aimed squarely at the rental fleet, and they sit at the upper end of what most NZ hire yards stock without going to specialist territory. The SJ82 T gives you a 24.99m platform height (88ft work height); the SJ86 T adds a 1.68m articulating jib and pushes platform height to 26.21m. Beyond that you're into the boutique 38m-plus units that come out for stadium roofs and silos. Below that, you're back into the SJ61/66 range that most jobs actually need.

So who is the 80-foot class for, and how do these two Skyjack units stack up?

What you're actually getting

Both units share the same chassis, same 74HP (55kW) Deutz TD2.9L4 diesel, same 2.49m stowed width, same 3.00m stowed height, same 11m wheelbase, and the same 45% gradeability. They also share the same Tier 4 Final / Stage V emissions territory, although Skyjack has gone the SMARTORQUE route of running a smaller engine harder rather than bolting on the full DPF/SCR aftertreatment stack that bigger engines need to meet emissions. That's a real consideration for hire companies in NZ where machines spend long periods sitting on yards between jobs, and DPF regen cycles are a known headache.

The headline difference between the two is the jib. The SJ86 T's 1.68m jib articulates +65° / -60°, which is what gives you the up-and-over capability you need for getting platform workers over parapets, around roof overhangs, or down into voids. The SJ82 T doesn't have a jib, so its working envelope is a straight reach. That's a meaningful distinction when specifying a unit for a hire fleet. The SJ86 T is a more versatile machine for difficult building geometry, while the SJ82 T is the cleaner choice when you mostly need straight-up reach and don't want to pay for a jib you won't use.

Horizontal reach is 22.10m on the SJ82 T and 23.42m on the SJ86 T. Platform capacity is 340kg (750lb) restricted or 227kg (500lb) at full extension, on both units, which translates to two or three personnel rated at the 12.5m/s (28mph) maximum wind rating. That capacity is lower than the SJ61/66 T+ siblings, which carry 454kg (1,000lb), and reflects the longer reach. At 26m up you're trading payload for height, and that's true of every boom in this class.

The Skyjack design pitch

Skyjack positions itself as the rental-focused brand. That positioning shows up in a few specific places worth flagging.

The relay-based control system with colour-coded and numbered wiring is genuinely useful. Anyone who's tried to fault-find a CANbus boom from a competitor at 4pm on a Friday will appreciate being able to trace a wire by colour and number rather than waiting on a laptop diagnostic. It also makes hire-fleet maintenance more straightforward for technicians who aren't brand-specialists. Bear in mind, though, that the trade-off is fewer of the diagnostic data points you get with CAN-based systems, which is why Skyjack offers ELEVATE telematics as an option to pull engine and machine data out.

The AXLDRIVE system is a true mechanical 4WD with an oscillating steer axle, operator-controlled locking rear differential, and a limited-slip front differential. Combined with 45% gradeability and 410mm (16in) ground clearance, this is a genuine rough-terrain unit. For NZ work that means viaduct construction, wind farm builds in the Manawatū or Waikato, motorway widening on uneven ground, or any of the rural infrastructure projects where the slab-paved site is the exception. Wet disc spring-applied hydraulic-release (SAHR) brakes on both axles are standard, which is the right specification for a machine of this weight and gradeability.

EASYDRIVE direction sensing is a small feature with a disproportionate safety benefit. The drive function reads the orientation of the turret relative to the chassis, so pushing the joystick forward moves the platform in the direction it's facing, not in some abstract chassis direction. Anyone who's trained an operator on a boom where the platform is over the rear of the chassis, and "forward" on the joystick means "backward in the world", knows why this matters. It cuts the most common cause of low-speed boom crashes, which is the operator getting disoriented during repositioning.

Hypothetical use cases

To put the spec sheet in context, here are four NZ scenarios where these units would earn their hire rate.

Cladding inspection on a 7-storey commercial building, central Auckland. The building owner needs a façade inspector to physically check sealant joints around windows on all four elevations. Total inspection height is roughly 22m. Pavement and traffic management make a scaffold prohibitively expensive and slow; a tower crane isn't justified. The SJ82 T's 22.10m horizontal reach lets you set up at one corner of the site and traverse the platform across the full elevation without repositioning the chassis on the live street. The 360° continuous turret rotation matters here: you can swing from one elevation to the next without re-stowing. The SJ82 T is the right pick over the SJ86 T because the façade is flat, you don't need the jib, and you save on hire cost.

Wind turbine maintenance, mid-Canterbury. A maintenance contractor needs platform access to inspect blade attachment hardware at hub height on a 30m-rotor turbine sited on rolling farmland. The hub itself is too high for an 86-footer, but pre-erection nacelle work, ground-mounted electrical cabinet maintenance, and tower base inspection all need a sub-30m boom that can self-propel across paddock between turbines. The SJ86 T at 17.5 tonnes is on the heavy side for soft ground, so foam-filled flotation tyres and ground mats are needed, but the 4WD and 45% gradeability handle the access tracks. The jib is useful here because nacelle hatches and tower-side inspection points are not always directly above the chassis position.

Bridge soffit inspection, SH1 motorway overpass. An NZTA-contracted bridge inspector needs to visually inspect the underside of a concrete overpass deck and the bearing pads at each pier. The deck soffit is at 8m above road level, but the inspector needs to work over the edge of the embankment, with the chassis positioned on the shoulder. The SJ86 T's jib is the deciding feature: it lets the platform articulate downward to look up under the deck from below the deck level, which a straight telescopic can't do. Combined with traffic management on a single lane closure, this is a textbook jib-boom job. The 26.21m platform height is far more than you need, but the jib articulation and 23.42m horizontal reach are what matter.

Silo cleaning and inspection, dairy plant in the Waikato. A food-grade dairy processing plant needs an internal inspection and cleaning of stainless steel silos at 24m. The silo roofs sit at around 25m and access is via a top hatch. Externally, an SJ86 T can set the platform on the silo roof level so workers can step off through the gate onto a temporary platform on the silo top, provided the rescue plan, harness anchorage, and fall-arrest setup are signed off. The platform's 0.91m x 2.44m deck is a comfortable working area for two operators with bagged equipment. The 110V AC outlet on the platform is useful here for inspection lights and small tools, and the Secondary Guarding Electrical anti-entrapment system is a tick in the box for confined-space-adjacent work where the operator is reaching forward into a hatch.

What's standard and what isn't

The standard specification on both units is reasonable for hire: SGE secondary guarding, overload sensing, tilt alarm with drive and lift cut-out, single-point emergency lowering, lockable power disconnect, 110V AC outlet on platform, lanyard attachment points, tri-entry sliding mid rails, 360° continuous turret rotation, and a 2-year Gold Leaf warranty with 5-year structural coverage.

The options list is where you need to pay attention. ELEVATE telematics is optional, not standard, despite Skyjack's marketing leading with it. The cold weather start kit (recommended for areas where monthly lows hit -10°C) and the arctic weather package (recommended for -18°C) are options most NZ hire fleets won't need; the South Island high country occasionally gets cold enough, but it's rare. The non-marking foam-filled tyres are an option worth specifying if the hire fleet does any work on finished concrete or sealed retail-precinct surfaces. The 3.5kW generator option (with hydraulic oil cooler) is useful for any platform-mounted power tool work and avoids the need to run a separate genset on a confined site.

The welder package, with its 12kW generator, 3-phase platform power, welder mount, and Lincoln V275-S, is a significant investment but turns the unit into a self-contained platform-welding station. For structural steel work on bridges, towers, or industrial fit-outs, this can be more efficient than running cables up to the platform from a ground-based welder.

Where these units fit in NZ training and licensing

Operators of these units in NZ work need to hold the relevant boom-type EWP qualification. AS/NZS 1418.10 covers the design standard for the equipment itself, and AS 2550.10 covers safe use. WorkSafe's Best Practice Guidelines for MEWPs is the working document any NZ trainer or fleet manager should have current.

A few practical training points specific to this class of machine. The high platform position means platform sway is more pronounced than on shorter units, and operators new to 80-foot class booms often misjudge their input-to-response timing. The drive-at-full-height capability is standard on both, but should be used at minimum speed and only on level, prepared ground. The 45% gradeability figure refers to the stowed unit, not the elevated one, and tilt alarms cut out drive and lift functions at 5.0° in any case. The SGE system on the platform railings is a backup; primary entrapment prevention is operator awareness and pre-task hazard identification.

Final thoughts

The SJ82 T and SJ86 T are competent units in a competitive class. The SMARTORQUE engine approach, the colour-coded wiring, and the relay-based controls are genuinely rental-friendly design choices that will reduce service callouts compared to more complex competitor units. The AXLDRIVE 4WD and 45% gradeability put them in the running for any NZ rough-terrain job that doesn't need the bigger 100ft-plus class.

The deciding factor between the two is the jib. If your typical job is straight-up reach against a building face, the SJ82 T is the right unit and you save the jib cost. If your work involves overhangs, parapets, bridge soffits, or any geometry where the platform needs to articulate below or behind the boom tip, the SJ86 T is worth the additional spend.

For NZ hire fleets specifying boom inventory, these are sensible additions to a fleet that already runs Skyjack scissors and smaller booms. The wiring and control commonality across the range pays off when service technicians are working across multiple machines on the same day.

Title: The Genie GR-26J: a vertical mast lift for jobs a boom lift can't quite do
Content:
There's a particular kind of job that frustrates both scissor lifts and boom lifts in roughly equal measure. The scissor can't get up and over anything. The boom can, but it's too heavy for the floor, too wide for the aisle, or it can't actually get close enough to the access point because of racking, fixed plant, or a wall in the way. The vertical mast lift sits in that gap, and the Genie GR-26J is one of the more useful machines in the category for indoor work where reach matters more than height.

This isn't a glowing endorsement of every spec — there are real trade-offs, and a GR-26J is not the right machine if you genuinely need to be 12m off the ground or carry three people and tools. But for the jobs it's designed for, it does things a boom lift physically cannot.

What you actually get

The GR-26J gives you a maximum platform height of 7.90m, which translates to a working height of 9.90m once you add the standard 2m for someone of average height standing on the platform. Horizontal reach is 2.65m, or 3.15m once you account for the operator's arm reach forward — Genie calls this the "working" horizontal reach. The up-and-over clearance is 6.70m, meaning you can get the platform over an obstacle 6.70m tall and reach down or across to whatever's behind it.

Width is 0.99m. That's the headline number for most people specifying one of these. It fits through a standard single doorway and down any aisle that a pallet jack can negotiate. Stowed length is 2.82m and stowed height is 1.99m, so it goes through a roller door without anyone needing to think about it.

The platform itself is 0.75m × 0.90m, which is small. Two people fit indoors; only one is permitted outdoors. Lift capacity is 200kg with the extension deck retracted, dropping to 136kg with it extended. That's enough for one operator and a reasonable kit of tools, but not enough to think of this as a materials-handling solution.

It runs on twelve 2V batteries giving 250Ah at 24V. There's an optional AC power outlet at the platform, which matters more than it sounds — see below. Drive is direct electric to the rear wheels, with front-wheel steer, and the tyres are 16 × 5 × 11.25 inch solid non-marking, so it won't streak a showroom floor or a finished concrete slab.

Weight is 2,650kg. That's the spec that gets it into places a boom lift can't go.

Where it earns its keep

Theatre and live event rigging

A theatre fly tower or a black-box studio is a brutal environment for access equipment. The floor is sprung timber in some cases, painted concrete in others, and you're frequently working over the seating, the apron, or set pieces that can't be moved. A 4-tonne articulating boom is not going on a sprung stage. The GR-26J at 2,650kg, with non-marking tyres and a floor pressure of 2,054 kg/m², is a much easier conversation with the venue manager.

You also rarely need huge horizontal reach in a theatre — you need to get straight up to a lighting bar, a flown set piece, or a rigging point in the grid. The 7.90m platform height covers most studio grids and the lower reaches of a proscenium fly tower. Where you do need to reach across — to a side-stage lighting position, or out from a catwalk anchor point to a unit hung 2m out — the 350° turntable rotation and 140° vertical jib articulation give you the angles. The jib means you can drop the platform down past a horizontal obstacle once you're up there, which is the move that makes vertical masts useful for grid work rather than just bar work.

The AC power option at the platform matters here. Plugging a soldering iron, a DMX tester, or a 12V scroller power supply in at the platform rather than running a lead up the mast is the difference between a 10-minute repair and a 30-minute one.

Maintenance of overhead services in distribution warehouses

This is the bread-and-butter use case. You've got a 7m high warehouse with racking up to about 6m, and somewhere up there is an HVAC duct, a sprinkler valve, an LED high-bay fitting, or a section of conduit that needs attention. The fitting itself is over the racking, not over the aisle.

A boom lift will get you to the height, but you can't drive it close enough — the racking takes up the aisle floor. Even with a slim electric boom (something like a Genie Z-30/20N at about 1.1m wide), you've still got the chassis sitting in the aisle and a long boom trying to articulate over the top of the racking. The boom geometry often doesn't suit it: you're either reaching too far horizontally to clear the racks, or you can't get the right downward angle to drop the platform into the gap behind them.

The GR-26J handles this differently. You drive into the aisle, raise the mast straight up to clear the racking, then use the 2.65m horizontal reach to extend across the top and down the other side, with the jib doing the final vertical adjustment. The up-and-over clearance of 6.70m is the spec to focus on here — that's the height of obstacle the machine can reach over.

Floor loading is also a real issue in distribution centres with mezzanines or upper-level offices. At 2,054 kg/m² occupied floor pressure, the GR-26J will go onto floors a boom lift can't. Always check the floor rating against the actual occupied pressure rather than the gross weight, because it's the pressure under the tyres that matters.

Gantry crane and overhead service inspection

A factory with a 5- or 10-tonne overhead travelling crane usually has the rails at around 7–8m, and the crane itself sits another 1–2m above that. Getting up to the rails for inspection, lubrication, festoon cable work, or limit switch adjustment is awkward.

The GR-26J gets the operator up to crane rail level for most installations. The narrow chassis lets you get between machinery on the factory floor rather than needing to clear an aisle wide enough for a boom. The up-and-over reach lets you get the platform past the side of the crane bridge to access the carriage or the festoon track, which is where most of the maintenance work actually happens.

One thing to bear in mind: the gantry crane itself must be locked out and tagged out before you bring the lift anywhere near the rails. The lift's working envelope and the crane's travel path will overlap, and a crane operator who doesn't know there's a maintenance lift up at rail level is the precondition for a fatality. That's a procedural issue rather than a machine issue, but it's the most common way overhead service work goes wrong.

Window and façade work where there's racking against the wall

Retail, big-box, and some warehouse buildings have racking, shelving, or fixed display fixtures running up against the windows on the inside. Cleaning, replacing, or sealing those windows from the inside means getting over the racking with a person and equipment.

A boom lift can't get over racking that's pushed against a wall — there's no aisle to drive into on the wall side. A scissor lift puts you in the aisle but you can't reach across the top of the racks. The GR-26J drives into the aisle on the open side of the racking, raises to clear the top, and reaches horizontally to the glazing. With the jib articulation, you can drop the platform down into the gap between the back of the racking and the window.

Same principle applies to atrium glazing accessed from a mezzanine, internal feature lighting hung behind a structural element, or signage on a wall behind fixed display fixtures.

What the GR-26J is not

A few honest limits.

It's not an outdoor machine in any serious sense. The spec allows outdoor use, but with a 0.99m width and 1.2m wheelbase, it's tippy on uneven ground, and the outdoor occupancy drops to one person. Gradeability is rated at 25%, but that's a stowed-drive figure on a hard surface, not a guidance to use it on rough ground. If you've got an outdoor task at 8m height and any wind exposure, you want a different machine.

It's not a high-reach machine. At 7.90m platform height, it covers a lot of indoor industrial and commercial work, but if you need to reach 10m or 12m, look at the larger vertical masts (Genie's own GR-30J or GR-35J) or at electric booms.

It's not a load-carrying platform. The 200kg capacity (136kg with the extension out) means one operator and modest tools. If the task involves carrying a 50kg fitting up to height along with the operator and a toolbox, you're at the limit before you start.

And the platform is small. Two people indoors is technically allowed, but if both people are doing anything that requires elbow room — a two-person electrical pull, for example — it's tight. For most jobs it's a single-operator machine.

Title: Tower Crane
Content: A staple of city skylines, anchored to the ground to lift heavy materials to extreme heights during skyscraper construction.

Title: Stacker Crane
Content: Computer-controlled automated cranes utilized in high-density automated storage and retrieval systems (ASRS).

Title: Carry Deck Crane
Content: A small, four-wheeled crane with a 360-degree rotating boom and a flat deck for transporting materials over short distances.

Title: Crawler Crane
Content: Equipped with tracks instead of wheels, providing exceptional stability and mobility on soft, unpaved construction sites.

Title: Floating Crane
Content: Massive cranes mounted on specialized barges or ships, used for bridge building or salvaging sunken vessels.

Title: Jib Crane
Content: A compact crane with a horizontal boom attached to a wall or pillar, ideal for localized lifting in workstations.

Title: Truck-Mounted Crane
Content: A crane mounted directly onto a standard truck bed, offering maximum mobility and quick setup times on public roads.

Title: Rough Terrain Crane
Content: A mobile crane with oversized tires and four-wheel drive, engineered specifically for off-road construction environments.

Title: Mobile Crane
Content: A versatile crane with a telescopic or lattice boom mounted on a wheeled or tracked chassis for easy transport.

Title: Gantry Crane
Content: Similar to an overhead crane but supported by its own legs traveling along ground-level rails, common at shipping ports.

Title: Crawler Tower Crane
Content: A hybrid combining the high vertical reach of a tower crane with the tracked mobility of a crawler crane.

Title: Overhead Crane
Content: Found in factories, featuring a parallel runway with a traveling bridge used to lift heavy manufacturing loads.

Title: Railroad Crane
Content: Designed with flanged wheels for use exclusively on railway tracks for maintenance and derailment recovery.

Title: Deck Crane
Content: Permanently installed on ships and cargo vessels for loading and unloading freight at ports lacking shore equipment.

Title: All-Terrain Crane
Content: A hybrid crane combining highway mobility with the rugged, off-road capabilities of a rough terrain crane.

Title: Harbor Crane
Content: Large-scale, high-capacity cranes stationed permanently at docks to rapidly load and unload container ships.

Title: Telescopic Handler
Content: Resembles a forklift but functions like a crane, featuring a telescopic boom that extends forwards and upwards.

Title: Aerial Crane
Content: Heavy-lift helicopters adapted to carry massive loads to remote or otherwise inaccessible locations.

Title: Level Luffing Crane
Content: A shipyard crane that automatically keeps its hook at a constant level while the boom moves inward or outward.

Title: Loader Crane
Content: A hydraulically powered articulated arm fitted to a truck that folds down compactly; used for loading cargo.

Title: Privacy policy
Content:
Overview

This website, dttraining.co.nz (referred to throughout this document as the "Site"), is the intellectual property of DT Driver Training Ltd ("we", "us", "our"), copyright 2010–2025. This Privacy Policy explains what personal data we collect from users of the Site, under what circumstances we collect it, how we store and use it, and what rights you have in relation to that data. This policy applies exclusively to information gathered through your use of the Site itself. It does not govern how any third party handles your data, and it does not apply to information gathered through any offline interaction with us or our affiliated organisations.

Our foundational approach to privacy is straightforward: what you do on the Site is your business. Your activity and results are only visible to people you have explicitly authorised to see them, or where applicable to the person or organisation that created your account on your behalf. We do not make your data publicly visible, sell it to advertisers, or share it in ways beyond what this policy describes.

If you choose not to create a user account, nothing from your visit is stored once your session ends. If you register your own account, you are in control of what gets shared and with whom and you can withdraw that access at any time. If a third party (such as an employer or driving instructor) invites you to use the Site, that party will be able to see your usage and results. The Site, all its content, any branded or custom URLs it appears under, and all personal information collected from its users, are the sole property of DT Driver Training Ltd.

This Privacy Policy forms part of the overall Terms and Conditions governing your use of the Site. It applies only to dttraining.co.nz and does not extend to any external websites including sites that link to us, or sites we link to. Furthermore, this policy covers how we handle your information. If your access to the Site was arranged through an employer or another organisation, that organisation may have its own separate data policies governing how they store, access, modify, or retain any information they have access to through their use of the Site.

Your Consent

By accessing and using the Site, you are indicating your acceptance of this Privacy Policy and giving your consent for us to collect and use your personal information in the manner described here. If you do not agree with any part of this policy, we recommend that you do not use the Site or provide us with any personal information.

What Information We Collect and Why

You can browse parts of the Site and take practice tests without providing any personal data at all. However, some features and services require us to collect additional information in order to function properly. Whenever we do collect personal data, it will have been provided directly by you typically when you complete a registration form, place an order, or fill in a survey. The types of information this might include are your full name, mailing or billing address, email address, phone number, gender, and any stated preferences. We may retain this information for future reference in connection with your account or purchases.

In some cases, another user may invite you to create an account on the Site or share their data with you. No personal information relating to you is stored by us until you actually create that account.

To give a clear picture of what data is retained and who can see it, here is a breakdown by account type:

Visitor (not logged in): Anyone can visit the Site and take car, motorbike, heavy vehicle, and tourist tests without creating an account. Your test results are stored temporarily during your active session only and are not retained once you leave. If you choose to email yourself a score, that data is held briefly while the email is being sent, then discarded.

User (free account holder): A User is someone who has voluntarily created a free account. We store your email address and a hashed version of your password, along with your five most recent test results and any optional profile information you have chosen to add.

Trainee (invited by a manager): Trainees are added to the platform by a Manager or Account Holder within an organisation. The Site stores their test results, login timestamps, and account activity data so that the supervising Manager can monitor progress. Additional information such as licence type, Training Log entries, and Qualifications records is stored if and when it is entered. Any data added to a Trainee's profile either by the Trainee or by the Manager at time of invitation is also retained.

Independent Trainee (self-funded): Independent Trainees purchase their own course licences rather than being invited through an organisation. Their full test results are saved unless they choose to delete them. An Independent Trainee may optionally grant a Manager access to view their name, email address, licence information, saved test results, and Training Log and Qualifications entries.

Manager: Managers are authorised users within an organisation who can view the data of Trainees or Independent Trainees who have granted them access, or whose access has been approved by an Account Holder.

Account Holder: The Account Holder sits at the top of the organisational hierarchy within a given account. They oversee Managers and Trainees, and have visibility over all information that Managers can see, across all users in their account.

In addition to the above, the Site stores a secure token issued by our payment processor, Windcave. This token allows you to save your payment method for future use without your actual credit card details ever being held on our servers. All payment processing takes place on Windcave's infrastructure, not ours.

Data Collected Automatically Through Site Use

Account information: When you create an account, we collect your email address and a password. Optionally, you can add further details such as your name, postal address, employer, a backup email address, your driver licence number, NSN, date of birth, and other profile fields.

Billing information: We use Windcave as our third-party payment processor. We do not store any payment card details or personally identifiable financial information on our own servers.

Usage and activity data: When you complete a test, we save the results so you can review them later. If you enter licence type information or fill in the training records sections, that data is also stored under your account.

Creating and Managing Your Account

When registering for an account, you are required to provide accurate, current, and complete information. You are solely responsible for keeping your account password confidential and for all activity that takes place under your account. You must not attempt to access another user's account without their explicit permission.

If you become aware that your account has been accessed without your authorisation, please contact us immediately. In the event your password has not been shared with anyone else and you still suspect unauthorised access, your device may have been compromised by spyware or a keylogger we recommend running up-to-date anti-spyware software as a precaution. DT Driver Training Ltd will never install any software on your device, and we will never ask for your password.

Cookies

When you visit the Site, a cookie will be placed on your device automatically. Cookies serve several purposes: they help us compile anonymised statistics about how the Site is used, they keep you logged in between pages, and they store temporary session data that is necessary for the Site to function correctly. In all of these cases, the cookies are not used to personally identify you.

We also work with third-party services including Google Analytics, which automatically records certain technical details about your visit including your IP address, browser type, and the pages you navigate to. We use New Relic to monitor the health and performance of our servers. These services operate independently and may track your usage to varying degrees in accordance with their own privacy policies.

How We Use the Information We Collect

Every piece of information we collect serves one of two purposes: to operate the Site effectively, or to improve it over time. More specifically, data is used to:

  • Authenticate your identity and enable you to log in securely
  • Identify which features and content are most frequently used, so we can prioritise improvements in those areas
  • Investigate technical issues, inefficiencies, and potential misuse or fraudulent activity
  • Respond to support enquiries and communicate with you through in-app notifications and email
  • Ensure the Site continues to serve users effectively as it evolves

We do not use your personal data for advertising profiling, and we do not sell it to third parties.

Email Communications

By using the Site you agree to receive certain operational emails from us. These are service-related messages covering things like planned maintenance windows, outages, changes to how the Site functions, or alerts when you are approaching a usage limit or renewal date. These messages are considered a fundamental part of the service and cannot be opted out of.

From time to time, we may also send you emails about new features, product updates, or other news relevant to the Site. Unlike the service emails above, these marketing-style communications are entirely optional. You can unsubscribe from them at any time using the link included in any such email, or by contacting us directly.

Deleting Your Account

The following account deletion information applies to both the website and the DT Driver Training app, which is available on both the Apple App Store and Google Play.

Managers can remove a Trainee's account immediately and permanently by first removing the Trainee from their course and then selecting Delete Permanently. This action removes all records associated with that Trainee's account with no recovery option.

Account Holders, or Managers who have been granted the relevant permissions, can permanently remove other Managers by navigating to Manage > Managers and clicking Delete.

If you are a business Account Holder, a free account holder, or an Independent Trainee who has purchased a course licence, you will need to contact us directly to request deletion of your account and associated data. Please use the contact form on our website to submit this request. We aim to process all deletion requests within one business day. Please be aware that once an account is deleted, all data associated with it is permanently removed and cannot be recovered. Before submitting a deletion request, we strongly recommend downloading any documents or certificates you may need for your own records.

Your Responsibilities

You are responsible for ensuring that the device and software you use to access the Site are technically compatible with the Site's requirements, and that your system is appropriately protected. This includes maintaining up-to-date antivirus and security software. While we take every reasonable precaution on our end, we are not able to guarantee that files downloaded from the Site are entirely free from malware, viruses, or other code with potentially harmful properties. You access and download such material at your own risk.

Sharing and Disclosure

We treat your personally identifiable information including your name and email address with care and will not share or disclose it to outside parties except in the following circumstances:

  • We are legally required to do so by a valid court order, law enforcement request, or applicable regulation
  • Our development and technical team members may access account data as part of their work maintaining and improving the Site however, they do not have access to credit card or payment information
  • We may publish aggregated, anonymised data for general interest for example, statistics about which test questions users find most challenging

We do not sell, rent, or trade your personal information with third-party marketers or data brokers.

Security

We take the protection of your information seriously and apply reasonable technical and organisational measures to guard against unauthorised access, loss, misuse, or disclosure. Sensitive data such as your login credentials is encrypted in transit using SSL (Secure Socket Layer) technology. We follow widely accepted industry standards for protecting personal data.

That said, no digital system is completely immune to risk. No internet transmission and no digital storage solution is entirely secure or error-free, and we cannot make absolute guarantees in this regard. We encourage users to use strong, unique passwords and to contact us promptly if they suspect any security issue with their account.

Use by Children

The Site is primarily designed for users who are 15 years of age and older, as this is the minimum age at which someone in New Zealand can begin practising for a learner licence. The educational content on the Site is accessible to people of all ages, and we do not have age verification systems in place. Parents and guardians should be aware of this when allowing younger users to access the Site.

Updates to This Policy

We reserve the right to revise and update this Privacy Policy from time to time. When changes are made, the updated version becomes effective immediately upon publication and supersedes all prior versions. We do not directly notify users when this policy is updated, so we encourage you to review it periodically. Continued use of the Site following any changes constitutes your acceptance of the revised policy.

Contacting Us

If you have any questions about this Privacy Policy, how your data is handled, or would like to make a request regarding your personal information, please visit our contact page for details on how to reach us.

Title: Terms and conditions
Content:
Terms and Conditions

Last Updated: June 5, 2026

1. Acceptance of Terms and Scope

Welcome to https://dttraining.co.nz/ (the "Site"). These Terms and Conditions constitute a binding, lawful contract between you (the individual user, corporate learner, or representative entity) and DT Driver Training Ltd (“we”, “us”, “our”), operating as a proud member of the TR Group Site network. By accessing, browsing, interacting with, or creating an account on this Site, or by downloading and interfacing with our mobile applications available via the Apple App Store and Google Play Store, you express absolute and unreserved agreement to these Terms and Conditions in full.

If you do not accept, understand, or agree to be governed by every provision outlined within this document, you must immediately terminate your session and cease all utilization of our digital platforms, software modules, and corporate interfaces. These terms govern all facets of our virtual learning tools, educational systems, testing simulators, and financial billing mechanics.

2. Purpose of Services and Legal Disclaimers

Title: DMCA
Content:
DMCA & Copyright Infringement Policy

We respect and protect intellectual property rights. In accordance with the Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA), we strictly oppose any unauthorized distribution or infringement of copyrighted material on our platform. Our policy is to promptly address and respond to formal notices of alleged copyright violations that comply with legal standards.

If you believe that your copyrighted material has been used on our website without authorization, you may file a formal takedown request by submitting a notice through our Contact Us page.

Required Information for Infringement Claims

To ensure your claim can be processed efficiently, your written DMCA notice must include the following details:

  • Authorized Signature: A physical or electronic signature of the copyright owner or a person legally authorized to act on their behalf.
  • Identification of the Work: A clear, precise description of the copyrighted work you claim has been infringed, allowing us to easily verify ownership.
  • Location of Infringement: The exact URL(s) or locations on our website where the allegedly infringing material is hosted.
  • Contact Information: Your complete contact details, including a physical mailing address, telephone number, and active email address.
  • Good Faith Statement: A formal statement confirming that you believe, in good faith, that the disputed use of the material is not authorized by the copyright owner, their agent, or the law.
  • Accuracy Statement: A statement made under penalty of perjury that the information provided in your notice is accurate and that you are authorized to act on behalf of the exclusive copyright owner.
Legal Notice: Under federal law, any individual who knowingly and materially misrepresents that material on our site is infringing a copyright may be held legally liable for damages and associated legal costs.

Our Takedown & Review Procedure

Upon receiving a valid, fully complete DMCA notice, we will immediately initiate an internal investigation. If the claim is found to be legitimate, we will promptly remove or restrict access to the targeted content.

As mandated by law, we will notify the user or third party who originally posted or hosted the disputed content. We also maintain a strict internal policy regarding repeat offenders, reserving the right to permanently terminate website access or user accounts for individuals who repeatedly violate copyright terms.

Fair Use Considerations & Claims Processing

Before submitting a request, we strongly advise you to consider whether the disputed content constitutes "Fair Use" (such as critique, education, parody, or news reporting). We reserve the right to legally contest any groundless or abusive DMCA notifications, and accepting notices does not waive our right to challenge improper claims.

Indemnification

By submitting a copyright infringement notice, you acknowledge that you may be held liable for legal damages, administrative expenses, and attorney fees incurred by us if it is determined that you willfully misrepresented a copyright violation.

Title: Cookie Policy
Content:
Cookie Policy

This Cookie Policy explains how DT Driver Training uses cookies and comparable tracking technologies to personalize, protect, and optimize your experience on our website (dttraining.co.nz). By utilizing our training platform, you consent to our deployment of these technologies as outlined below.

1. Understanding Cookies

Cookies are compact alphanumeric text files that are stored directly within your web browser or device storage when you access digital platforms. They serve to recognize your specific hardware or browser settings, ensuring a seamless experience when returning to our site, saving preference data, and analyzing visitor interactions.

We use both first-party cookies (set directly by us) and third-party cookies (deployed by specialized analytical or structural partners) to deliver secure training services.

2. The Categories of Cookies We Use

To run an effective learning management system and training platform, we categorize our cookies into the following specific brackets:

  • Essential & Structural Cookies: These are strictly required to operate the infrastructure of our site. They control user authentication, account security, progress preservation across training modules, and securely route traffic. Disabling these will cause parts of the platform to break.
  • Functional & Preference Cookies: These help our system recall custom settings you have chosen, such as language filters, layout configurations, text sizes, or progress preferences, minimizing the need to re-configure them on subsequent visits.
  • Performance & Analytics Cookies: We utilize these to gather aggregate, non-personally identifiable data on how learners navigate our platform. This information tells us which training modules are most popular, where users face technical blockages, and how we can refine our course interfaces.
  • Operational & Administrative Cookies: For corporate and fleet accounts, these cookies allow manager dashboards to function correctly, ensuring that trainee logs, compliance documentation, and multi-user tracking operate reliably.

3. Managing and Controlling Your Preferences

You maintain ultimate authority over how cookies interact with your personal computer or mobile device. Most modern internet browsers give you the ability to block, remove, or limit cookie collection through their native settings menus.

To adjust these settings, look into your browser's documentation (typically found under "Settings," "Privacy," or "Preferences"). Please be aware that restricting or deleting essential operational cookies may prevent you from logging into your trainee profile, tracking course scores, or downloading certificates.

4. Updates and Revisions to This Policy

We may periodically update this Cookie Policy to reflect technical, operational, or legal developments within our driver training infrastructure. We recommend reviewing this document regularly to remain informed about how we safeguard your browsing environment.

5. Reach Out to Us

If you have any questions or require structural clarification regarding how we use tracking technologies on dttraining.co.nz, please get in touch with our support team directly via our Contact Us page.

Title: Tourist
Content:
Driving in New Zealand

If you are hiring a car, motorhome or campervan you'll need to have a current, valid driver's licence. You must not have received a disqualification or suspension in New Zealand. You must have entered New Zealand less than 12 months ago and not have a New Zealand licence. If your licence is not in English you will need an accurate translation to English. Read our guide here on  driving as a tourist in New Zealand.

Visiting for work

If you are visiting New Zealand for work, either on behalf of an overseas company or on your own visa obtaining a job in New Zealand (including au pairs and seasonal workers), the tourist quiz is an excellent start to learning the Road Code but you might also want to check out the full Road Code tests in the Car section. While insurance isn't compulsory in New Zealand it is recommended that you check you are insured because an accident could leave you with serious debt to repay.

Students

If you are an international student wanting to drive in New Zealand, check the age limits for your class of licence - you cannot own a full licence here until you are 18 years old unless you have passed an approved advanced driving course. If you stay more than 12 months here you will need to get a New Zealand licence. However, if you go back to your home country then return, you can drive again for 12 months on your existing overseas licence. Your education provider should be able to provide additional knowledge about living in New Zealand. Read our full guide for international student drivers here.

Road rules overview

We drive on the left-hand side using vehicles with the steering wheel on the right-hand side.

New Zealand has a set of give way rules which describe the priority of traffic at intersections and roundabouts. At T-intersections you must give way to all traffic travelling across the top of the T, or turning in front of you. If you are on the top of the T turning right you must give way to traffic coming straight through or turning left. At a crossroads (four-way intersection), give way to traffic coming straight through or from your right.

Roundabouts are driven clockwise. If you are turning left at a roundabout, indicate left as you approach. If you are passing straight across a roundabout, don't indicate as you approach. You should indicate left just after you pass the exit before the one you want to take. If you are turning right, approach the roundabout in the right-hand lane signalling right, then signal left just after you pass the exit before the one you want to take.

If an intersection is controlled by a stop sign it is compulsory to stop.

Speed limits

The default open road speed limit is 100kph and the default urban limit is 50kph. However, there are stretches of rural road which are 80 or 90kph where the accident rate has proven to be higher. Shared pedestrian zones in the city are 10kph. Road works on all roads except motorways have a speed limit of 30kph, with 70-80kph on motorways. The speed limit past a school bus that has stopped to drop off or pick up children is 20kph.

While road speed limit signs are denoted by a red circle, advisory speed limit signs are black numbers on a yellow background. These indicate the advised maximum speed in dry weather for a corner. Speed limits always end in 0 whereas advisory limits end in 5.

Parking

Parking signs are blue and will give the length of time parking is allowed, the types of vehicles that are allowed there and the times the parking is in force. If no times are specified, the parking limit is in force between 8am and 6pm. Clearways are stretches of road where you are not allowed to park between certain times, for example in rush hour. A dashed yellow line means you are not allowed to park on that stretch of road at any time.

Distances

Distances are measured in kilometres. On rural roads, expect your average to be 70-80kph, not 100kph. It can take longer than you expect to drive places in New Zealand, especially at certain times of the year when there are more tourists or more agricultural or logging vehicles on the road. Some areas will have a lot of logging truck activity or agricultural vehicles.

Alcohol and drug usage

It is illegal to drive if you are affected by drugs of any kind (including legal medications for illnesses like colds and flu). The alcohol limit is 250mcg per litre of breath, or 50mg/100ml of blood (0.05%). Check the insurance policy from your rental car company or your travel insurance as you are unlikely to be covered if you have an accident and you are driving under the influence of alcohol or drugs.

Emergency vehicles

Police cars have red and blue flashing lights. Ambulances and fire engines have red flashing lights. Maintenance vehicles have orange flashing lights. You must make way for police, fire and ambulance emergency vehicles when their lights and sirens are activated. Don't make any sudden moves like braking hard. Move left if possible and give them space.

Railway crossings

Most railway crossings on busy roads are controlled by lights and/or barrier arms, but around half of New Zealand's rail crossings are in rural areas and are controlled only by give way or stop signs. Take extra care when approaching these crossings. Ensure that you can see each way up the track and that there is no train coming before you cross. When crossing a railway crossing in a busier area you must make sure that there is room for your vehicle on the other side of the crossing before you cross.

Road signs

Most road signs follow international conventions but there are many subtle differences between those in New Zealand and those in the UK or America.

Road conditions in New Zealand

New Zealand has very variable road conditions from 5-lane motorways at one extreme to roads that are beaches at the other extreme. The large rural area means that many roads are unsealed (gravel) and can be narrow. Motorways don't exist outside of the main centres, although there are dual carriageways and expressways in some areas.

Many of New Zealand roads have limited opportunities for overtaking. Passing lanes and slow vehicle bays are provided on busier roads.

Winter can bring snow and ice throughout the South Island and in the North Island on Desert Road and sections of high country such as the Napier-Taupo Highway and around the ski fields such as Turoa and Whakapapa. Check online before you leave.

Fatigue

When you arrive in New Zealand you will almost certainly suffer jet lag unless you have come from Australia. Take extra care when driving. Frequent breaks are important to help you recharge, as is keeping hydrated.

Hiring a motorbike

If you are hiring a motorbike while you are in New Zealand we strongly recommend using the motorbike section as there are specific guidelines for riding, plus rules around pillion passengers. You will need to hold a motorbike licence from your home country that permits you to drive a motorbike of the size and power that you want to hire here. Helmets are compulsory and you must ride with your headlight on at all times

Now you have read the rules, take the quiz to find out how much you know.

This website works on your computer, tablet or smartphone. Bookmark it on your smartphone and you can check the Road Code out while you are on the road, too.
